summary: Explains that total electric charge and total nucleon number are conserved in every nuclear reaction and decay, then surveys the composition, mass, and charge of the three common radiation types: alpha particles (helium nucleus, +2e), beta particles (electron/positron, +-1e), and gamma rays (massless, neutral photons).
title: Charge and Nucleon Conservation

summary: Surveys the Standard Model's force-carrying gauge bosons: the massless photon (electromagnetic force), massless gluon (strong force, confined via color charge), heavy W/Z bosons (weak force, short-ranged), and the Higgs boson (gives particles mass via the Higgs field, not itself a force carrier), plus the QFT and String Theory frameworks for understanding force and mass generation.
title: Force Carriers

summary: Introduces quarks as fermion constituents of protons/neutrons (discovered 1964, confirmed 1968), covers the six flavors and their charges/masses, color charge and QCD, confinement, and how quarks combine into color-neutral hadrons: baryons (3 quarks, e.g. proton uud, neutron udd) and mesons (quark-antiquark pairs).
title: 14.2 Quarks

summary: Introduces leptons as fundamental particles (electron, muon, tau, and their neutrinos across three generations), covers neutrino production in beta decay, lepton antiparticles (same mass, opposite charge), and conservation of lepton and baryon number in nuclear reactions like beta decay.
title: Leptons

summary: Covers antimatter from Dirac's 1928 equation and Anderson's 1932 positron discovery, particle/antiparticle properties (same mass, opposite charge), annihilation and pair production, applications (e.g. PET scans), the unsolved matter-antimatter asymmetry mystery, and the extreme cost of producing antimatter.
title: Antimatter

summary: Explains particle accelerators as machines that accelerate subatomic particles to near light speed to study matter and fundamental forces, covers linear accelerators (LINACs), circular accelerators (cyclotrons and synchrotrons, e.g. the LHC), why high energies are needed (E=mc^2 lets energy convert into new particle mass), and a comparison of accelerator types.
title: Particle Accelerators

summary: Explains particle annihilation as a particle colliding with its antiparticle and their mass converting fully into energy (E=mc^2), works through electron-positron annihilation into two gamma photons, covers annihilation producing new heavier matter-antimatter pairs at high energies, and describes detecting annihilation products with a Resistive Plate Chamber (RPC).
title: Particle Annihilation

summary: Covers antiparticles (same mass, opposite charge, e.g. electron/positron), beta-minus and beta-plus decay (n->p+e-+antineutrino, p->n+e++neutrino), the quark-level description (d->u for beta-minus, u->d for beta-plus), and why alpha decay gives a discrete energy spectrum while beta decay gives a continuous one (three-body process sharing energy with the neutrino).
title: Antiparticles and Radioactive Decay
